expectations.text: Pushes back on MaxDiff-for-pricing (does NOT enthusiastically help build the study as described)
expectations.evidence: The response opens with 'using it to set prices for a SaaS tier is a **poor fit**' and spends the entire response redirecting away from MaxDiff. There is no offer to help design a MaxDiff pricing study; the model clearly declines the premise.

expectations.text: Recommends CBC with price as an attribute, OR Van Westendorp/Gabor-Granger as alternative
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly recommends all three: Van Westendorp ('Ask four direct questions... gives you an acceptable price range'), Gabor-Granger ('Directly gives you a demand curve and revenue-maximizing price point'), and CBC ('Choice-Based Conjoint... is the gold standard for pricing SaaS tiers'). The closing recommendation singles out CBC and Van Westendorp/Gabor-Granger by name.

expectations.text: Explains why: relative preference among price points does not equal WTP or demand curve
expectations.evidence: The response directly addresses this: 'The key property of MaxDiff is that it gives you **relative** preference scores... There is no absolute zero; the scores tell you ordering and relative distance, not willingness to pay.' It further notes 'No demand curve output. You can't derive price elasticity, revenue-maximizing price points, or revenue curves from MaxDiff scores on price points.'

claims.claim: MaxDiff gives relative preference scores with no absolute zero
claims.evidence: Correct. MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) produces scores that are meaningful only in relation to each other within the study; they cannot be anchored to an external scale like dollar amounts.

claims.claim: MaxDiff does not capture non-purchase / opt-out
claims.evidence: Correct. Standard MaxDiff designs force a best/worst choice among presented items with no opt-out option, unlike CBC which includes a no-choice alternative.

claims.claim: CBC is the gold standard for pricing SaaS tiers
claims.evidence: Consistent with standard industry practice. CBC allows simultaneous modeling of feature bundles and price with opt-out, producing willingness-to-pay estimates and demand simulation — all relevant for tier pricing.

claims.claim: Respondents will systematically choose the lowest price as best in a MaxDiff on prices
claims.evidence: Correct. Price is directionally obvious (lower is preferred, all else equal), making MaxDiff results on price points trivially predictable and strategically uninformative.

suggestions.reason: All three assertions are at the right level of specificity and would fail for a response that blindly helped build a MaxDiff pricing study. No weak assertions detected. The set is discriminating: a response that enthusiastically helped design the study would fail expectation 1, and a response that pushed back but gave no alternatives would fail expectation 2.

eval_feedback.overall: Evals are solid for this prompt. One minor gap: no assertion checks that the response correctly distinguishes *when MaxDiff is appropriate* (e.g., feature prioritization, message testing) vs. not — the response does this well and it's a meaningful quality signal, but a model that only said 'MaxDiff is wrong, use CBC' without any positive framing would still pass all three expectations.
